item.title: 63% of US physicians now use AI for clinical decision support, up from 37% a year ago, Doximity's survey of 3,379 doctors finds
item.description: The shift from note-taking to decision-making happened in twelve months, three in four doctors hit a factual error in the past year, and most worry trainees will never build the skills to catch one.
item.content:encoded:
The shift from note-taking to decision-making happened in twelve months, three in four doctors hit a factual error in the past year, and most worry trainees will never build the skills to catch one.

Doximity's Doctor-Driven AI report, released on November 12 and based on a September survey of 3,379 US physicians across 20 specialties, finds that more than half of doctors now use AI every day and another third use it at least weekly. The number that matters is what they use it for: 63% now use AI for clinical decision support, up from 37% in the 2025 survey. Use for reviewing medical literature rose to 70% from just over half.

From paperwork to judgment

Until this year the physician AI story was ambient scribes and inbox drafting, tools that save time without touching the diagnosis. The Doximity data says that boundary has moved. Doctors are asking models about differential diagnoses, treatment alternatives and guideline updates; 81% say AI has taught them something they did not know, and 65% say it has helped develop their clinical skills. That is a different risk profile from a scribe. A scribe that errs produces a wrong note that a clinician reads; a decision-support tool that errs produces a wrong idea that a clinician may act on.

The survey is candid about error rates. Three in four physicians encountered at least one factual inaccuracy in AI output over the past year, and more than half say inaccuracies are the main reason they have ever cut back. At the same time, over a quarter say the effort they spend checking and correcting output has fallen compared with a year ago. Read those together: errors are common, and the verification habit is weakening as trust grows.

The trainee problem

The finding health-system leaders should sit with is about residents. 61% of physicians worry that trainees will lean on AI and fail to build their own clinical skills; nearly half worry about over-reliance generally; more than a quarter name skill erosion as the main thing limiting their own use. Medicine has been here before with calculators, imaging and order sets, and the historical pattern is that skills migrate rather than vanish. But the speed is new. A resident starting in July 2026 has never practised without a model that answers clinical questions in seconds.

Context and the counter-argument

Doximity's sample skews toward its own engaged users, and self-reported "use" ranges from a quick literature check to a treatment plan; the report does not distinguish. Most of the tools in question are general chatbots, not FDA-reviewed decision-support devices, which is why the FDA's still-unsettled position on generative AI in clinical workflows matters more than it did. The counter-argument is simply that physicians are professionals who are checking: the error-encounter rate shows doctors are catching mistakes, not missing them, and the survey records no claim of patient harm.

What to do

Health systems should offer a sanctioned tool with logging and PHI controls before trying to block consumer ones; the survey says blocking will fail. Credentialing and CME programmes should add verification as an explicit skill, with case reviews that include the AI output the clinician saw. Residency directors should decide now which tasks trainees do without a model for their first year. And vendors pitching clinical AI should expect buyers to ask for their factual-error rate on real queries, because three in four of the clinicians in the room have already seen one.

What to watch

The FDA's next move on generative clinical decision support; whether the AMA or specialty boards publish AI-use competencies for residents; and the 2027 edition of this survey, where the checking-effort number will tell you whether trust is being earned or assumed.

item.title: Gemini for healthcare: Google's agent reads Epic, Medicare rules and payer systems for seven launch customers; what to ask before you pilot it
item.description: Northwell has 400 people fighting insurance denials and wins 90% of them; Google wants both sides of that fight running on its agent. The economics, the safeguards and the questions a health system should put in writing.
item.content:encoded:
Northwell has 400 people fighting insurance denials and wins 90% of them; Google wants both sides of that fight running on its agent. The economics, the safeguards and the questions a health system should put in writing.

Google Cloud launched Gemini for healthcare on November 10 as a US preview. It is an agent built on Google's general Gemini agent that connects to the systems hospitals and insurers already run: electronic records from Epic and Oracle Health, billing platforms, federal Medicare coverage data and clinical guidelines from ASCO and the BMJ. It ships with five preset skills, among them summarising a medical record, preparing for an appointment, checking a patient's insurance benefits and preparing or reviewing a prior authorisation, and customers can build their own. Launch customers are Northwell Health, Highmark Health, HCA Healthcare, Optum, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, Hartford HealthCare and Stanford School of Medicine. Pricing is per seat or pay as you go, with no figures published.

What it does and does not touch

The agent reads records but cannot write to them; clinicians make any chart change. Every finding links to its source so staff can check it. Customers choose which models run which tasks, from Google, Anthropic or OpenAI, with simple administrative work routed to faster, cheaper models and complex clinical reasoning to stronger ones. Google says customer data is never used to train its foundation models. In a demonstration for Fortune, the agent compared an outside specialist's report with a patient's Epic chart in 35 seconds and flagged new lab results and a missed allergy. Seven partners announced the same day: GoodRx brings prescription prices into the agent, UiPath lets teams trigger its automations from it, Verato matches patient identities across systems, InterSystems connects its FHIR server, and Altimetrik, AuxoAI and Egen will do deployments. NextGen Healthcare support is due in the coming months.

The economics Google is selling

The numbers in Google's launch material are about paperwork, not diagnosis. Google's own Harris Poll study says clinicians lose nearly 28 hours a week to documentation and administration. The American Medical Association counts about 40 prior authorisations per physician per week, roughly 13 hours of physician and staff time, and 40% of practices employ people whose only job is handling them. Northwell's chief executive, John D'Angelo, told Fortune the system runs on a margin of 1% at best, that about 400 employees work solely on insurance denials, and that Northwell overturns more than 90% of them. Highmark says 78% of approved outpatient prior authorisations submitted digitally are already processed automatically and that a clinician reviews every case before a denial. The pitch, in other words, is to put the same agent on both sides of a transaction that currently employs thousands of people to argue with each other.

The counter-argument

If the agent makes it cheaper for a hospital to submit prior authorisations and cheaper for a payer to review them, the volume of both can rise without anyone's costs falling; the AMA's figures describe an arms race, and this is faster ammunition. The 35-second demonstration is a demonstration, not a controlled study. Errors in AI-generated clinical documentation are documented, including drug-name and diagnosis mistakes found in NHS records in August. And a read-only agent with access to Epic, Medicare datasets and payer portals under a single service identity is exactly the credential that the LLMjacking market, as the Railway post-mortem this week shows, now pays for.

What to ask before a pilot

Ask for the per-skill permission model: which systems each preset skill can read and whether a custom skill inherits more. Ask where the audit log of every record read lives, who can export it and how long it is retained. Ask which model vendor sees which data under the routing policy, and get all three named as sub-processors in the business associate agreement. Ask what the agent does when Epic and the outside report disagree, and who is told. Ask for a pilot design that measures staff hours per authorisation and per denial, turnaround time and overturn rate against a matched control, not a before-and-after. And ask the payer across the table whether they are running the same agent, because the answer changes what a faster submission is worth.

What to watch

Pricing once the preview ends; the first published outcome data from Northwell or Highmark; whether CMS's own prior-authorisation rules, which already set timelines for payers, treat agent-prepared submissions differently; and whether Epic, which the agent reads but which has its own AI roadmap, keeps the door open.

item.title: Oura pays $625 million for Counsel Health: a 70-person AI primary-care startup is now worth 17 times what it raised
item.description: A smart-ring maker that could not get its own IPO away is paying up for a chat-first clinic with physicians in the loop; the price says where consumer health AI is heading and what regulators will be watching.
item.content:encoded:
A smart-ring maker that could not get its own IPO away is paying up for a chat-first clinic with physicians in the loop; the price says where consumer health AI is heading and what regulators will be watching.

Oura, the Finnish smart-ring company, agreed on November 10 to acquire Counsel Health for $625 million. Counsel runs a chat-based medical service in which an AI assistant handles the conversation and hands off to a licensed physician for diagnosis and treatment over telehealth. The service has been available inside the Oura app since June. Counsel's chief executive, Muthu Alagappan, becomes Oura's chief clinical AI officer, its roughly 70 staff move across, and the companies expect to close before the end of 2027, which suggests a regulatory review of some length. The structure of the consideration was not disclosed.

The numbers

Counsel had raised about $36 million in total, including a $25 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and GV roughly a year ago, so the price is about 17 times invested capital. Oura itself was valued at $11 billion after a $900 million round in October 2025, reported $533 million of revenue for the September quarter, up 153% year on year, and expects about $1.75 billion for its fiscal year, up 92%. In October it indefinitely postponed an IPO that had targeted up to $2.2 billion, citing uncertainty in the listing market. It is paying more than a third of a year's revenue for a company with no disclosed revenue of its own.

For context, the digital-health exit market has been thin. Abridge, the ambient-scribe leader valued at $5.3 billion, confirmed layoffs this week. The large deals of the past year have been infrastructure and scribes, not care delivery. A consumer hardware company paying nine figures for a care-delivery team is a different signal: that the valuable asset is the clinical workflow and the physician network, not the model.

What Oura is actually buying

Oura's rings produce continuous biometric data, and the company has spent the year acquiring the pieces to act on it: Doublepoint for gesture control in March, Galen's AI health companion in April, now Counsel. The pattern is a path from a sleep score to a conversation to a prescription without leaving the app. Counsel already serves enterprise partners and will keep doing so, which gives Oura a business-to-business channel into employers and plans alongside its consumer base.

Alagappan has been explicit that Counsel keeps "physicians in the loop for clinical decisions." That is both a safety design and a regulatory one. Software that recommends a diagnosis or treatment without a clinician making the call risks being a medical device under FDA rules; software that organises the conversation and routes it to a doctor generally does not. Keeping the physician as the decision-maker lets the AI handle intake, triage and follow-up at scale without a clearance. The question for anyone copying the model is where that line sits when the AI's suggestion is, in practice, what the physician signs.

The counter-argument

Chat-first care has been tried by Babylon, which collapsed, and by a dozen telehealth companies whose unit economics never closed because physician time does not scale like software. Counsel's bet, and now Oura's, is that the AI absorbs enough of the encounter to change the ratio; nothing public yet shows that it does. Oura also has no history of running a regulated clinical service, in a year when state attorneys general and the FTC have both been active on health-app data. And the combination of continuous biometrics, medical chat and physician records in one company creates a dataset that will draw both the most lucrative partnerships and the most serious breach consequences in consumer health.

What to watch

The closing timetable and whether it draws an FTC second request; how Oura prices Counsel for ring owners versus the standalone membership; whether Hims & Hers, Function Health, Whoop or Apple respond with acquisitions of their own; what the combined privacy policy says about joining biometric and clinical data; and any state medical-board scrutiny of AI-led intake. For health systems, the practical question is whether Counsel's physicians refer into your network or around it.

item.title: Abridge cuts staff at a $5.3 billion valuation: what it says about the AI scribe market, and what health systems should ask
item.description: The best-funded company in ambient clinical documentation is flattening its organisation as the category commoditises; buyers mid-contract should get roadmap and support commitments in writing.
item.content:encoded:
The best-funded company in ambient clinical documentation is flattening its organisation as the category commoditises; buyers mid-contract should get roadmap and support commitments in writing.

Abridge confirmed on November 9 that it has laid off employees in what a spokesperson called an organisation-wide realignment intended to flatten the company. It did not say how many roles were affected or where; two people describing themselves as former employees, both with the company less than a year, posted on LinkedIn that the cuts came sooner than expected, and one layoff tracker reported a figure of around 90 that Abridge has not confirmed. The company said it was realigning from a position of strength, remains very well capitalised and still holds more than half of all the capital it has ever raised.

The company

Founded in Pittsburgh in 2018, Abridge became the reference name in ambient clinical documentation: software that listens to a patient visit and drafts the clinical note, with later extensions into automated billing and nursing documentation. Its 2025 Series E, led by Andreessen Horowitz, raised $300 million at a $5.3 billion valuation, and earlier rounds brought in Nvidia and Eli Lilly as investors. It is embedded in Epic's marketplace and has signed large academic health systems.

Why a leader trims at the top

Ambient scribing is the most widely deployed category of clinical AI, which is exactly its problem. The underlying speech and language models have become cheap and interchangeable, the electronic health record vendors have built or bought their own scribes, and Microsoft's Nuance has bundled one into a suite that many hospitals already license. When every vendor can transcribe accurately, the price per clinician falls toward what the EHR vendor charges, and the start-up that raised at 2024 growth multiples has to show margin. Flattening an organisation is what that looks like from the inside.

The realignment also hints at where Abridge thinks the next value is. The company's recent product moves have been toward revenue-cycle work, coding accuracy and nursing workflows rather than better transcription. Those are harder integrations with longer sales cycles, and they need a different mix of staff than a land-grab for clinician seats.

The counter-argument

A company holding more than half its lifetime funding after a $300 million round is not in distress, and small cuts after rapid hiring are routine in late-stage start-ups. Abridge still has the deepest health-system footprint of any independent scribe vendor and an Epic integration competitors cannot easily replicate. It is also possible the cuts reflect automation inside Abridge's own operations, which would be an uncomfortable but unsurprising outcome for an AI company. Without a disclosed number, the LinkedIn posts and a tracker's estimate are thin evidence of anything structural.

What health systems should ask

If you are mid-contract, ask Abridge in writing for the support staffing assigned to your account, a twelve-month product roadmap and the data-portability terms if you leave. Benchmark the price per clinician against what your EHR vendor would charge for its native scribe, including the integration cost you would avoid. Put coding accuracy and documentation time saved, not transcription word-error rate, at the centre of your evaluation, because that is where vendors are now competing and where the dollars are. And treat the next Abridge financing as the signal: a flat or down round would confirm that ambient documentation has become a feature, not a company.

item.title: The PATIENT AI Act draft: a third-party FDA review path and a Medicare pathway, comments due December 1
item.description: Senator Cassidy's discussion draft is the first serious attempt to legislate how clinical AI gets reviewed and paid for. FDA lawyers say the review title mostly duplicates what the agency can already do.
item.content:encoded:
Senator Cassidy's discussion draft is the first serious attempt to legislate how clinical AI gets reviewed and paid for. FDA lawyers say the review title mostly duplicates what the agency can already do.

Senator Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana physician who chairs the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, released a discussion draft on October 29 called the Protecting Americans Through Intelligent, Ethical, and Transparent Artificial Intelligence in Health Care Act, or PATIENT AI Act. It asks for stakeholder feedback by December 1. It is a draft, not a bill, and it has no co-sponsors yet. It is also the most complete legislative sketch so far of how the US might regulate and pay for AI in clinical care, which is why it deserves a close read now rather than when it is introduced.

What is in it

The draft runs to 19 sections across several titles covering privacy, cybersecurity, liability, transparency, workforce training, datasets, health IT and Medicare coverage and payment for AI services. Health systems and medical schools have focused on the workforce and coverage pieces: HHS would be told to identify ways AI can improve outcomes and operations and to build training resources for clinicians, and CMS would get a pathway to make coverage determinations for AI-based services.

The FDA title has drawn the sharpest technical reading. Section 201 would create a voluntary preliminary review of individual software components of "integrated devices", with FDA directed to rely more on prior related reviews, though components would not receive standalone authorisation. Section 202 writes a risk-based approach to premarket review of software devices into statute and lets manufacturers submit predetermined change-control plans for changes made while a 510(k) or PMA is still under review. Section 203 sets up an accredited third-party review programme for low- and moderate-risk software devices across 510(k), de novo and PMA submissions. Section 204 is a voluntary pilot to modernise postmarket surveillance, coordinated with CMS on payment.

The lawyers' critique

In an analysis published November 8, Steven Gonzalez and Jennifer Newberger of Hyman, Phelps & McNamara argue that Title II largely duplicates authority FDA already exercises. The agency already applies risk-based review; it already accepts predetermined change-control plans; it already runs a third-party review programme. Component review, they note, still leaves the manufacturer filing a full submission, so it is unclear what is gained, and the draft is silent on whether component reviews carry a user fee. Change plans filed mid-review could create version-control and deadline problems under the MDUFA performance goals. Their conclusion is that the draft could add procedure without shortening the path to market.

That critique matters because the industry's real complaint is not the absence of pathways but their speed and predictability. FDA has now authorised well over a thousand AI-enabled devices, almost all through 510(k). The recent example of UpDoc, an LLM-enabled insulin-dosing assistant cleared in December 2025 by pairing a conversational model with a deterministic, clinician-configured dosing engine and a conventional predicate, shows the existing route can accommodate generative AI when the intended use is narrow. What it does not do well is handle models that update frequently or systems whose clinical role is broad, and the draft's component and change-plan ideas are aimed at exactly that gap, however imperfectly.

Why the Medicare title may matter more

For most health-AI companies the binding constraint is not clearance but payment. A statutory CMS pathway for coverage of AI services would be the first general mechanism for reimbursing software that does clinical work, replacing today's patchwork of new technology add-on payments and a handful of CPT codes. Investors have been asking for this since 2023; it is the provision most likely to change which products get built.

What to watch

The December 1 comment deadline, and who files. Whether a Democratic co-sponsor emerges, which would signal the draft is headed for introduction rather than the archive. Whether the FDA title is trimmed to the pieces lawyers cannot find in current law, chiefly component review and user-fee treatment. And how the draft interacts with the state AI laws and the federal pre-emption fight that defined 2026's AI policy calendar.

item.title: OpenAI's BioBasicsBench: AI agents score 66.7% on routine lab work, and the failures are the story
item.description: A new 100-task benchmark tests whether AI can read gels, plates and microscopy like a bench scientist. The headline score is decent; the error cases show why nobody should hand it a pipette yet.
item.content:encoded:
A new 100-task benchmark tests whether AI can read gels, plates and microscopy like a bench scientist. The headline score is decent; the error cases show why nobody should hand it a pipette yet.

On November 6 OpenAI published BioBasicsBench, a benchmark built with the enzyme-design company Ligo Biosciences to test one narrow, important skill: can an AI agent look at the raw output of an everyday laboratory experiment and draw the right conclusion?

What it tests

The benchmark contains 100 tasks across five areas of routine wet-lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Instead of the clean figures that appear in published papers, the inputs are the messy artefacts a technician actually sees: gel images, colony plates, microscope fields, instrument readouts, including failed and ambiguous experiments.

Agents must return a structured conclusion, measurement or recommendation. A rubric awards partial credit for the numerical result, the reasoning, and, notably, for recognising when the evidence is not sufficient to support a conclusion at all.

The scores

OpenAI reports that GPT-6 Astra, at its highest reasoning setting, earned 66.7% of available credit, versus 43.8% for the earlier GPT-5.6 Sol. The post compares only OpenAI models and gives no human baseline, so the number says how far OpenAI's own models have moved, not how they compare with a trained technician.

The failures matter more

OpenAI's own write-up is unusually frank about error cases, and they are the useful part. In one colony-counting task the model merged neighbouring colonies, missed visible ones and marked empty agar, overcounting by about 12%, which would inflate a downstream efficiency estimate by the same amount. The pattern across failures is a correct observation paired with a wrong call. OpenAI's own summary: higher scores do not yet mean reliable judgement in the lab.

What this means for healthcare and life sciences

  • For lab teams: these agents are approaching usefulness as a second reader that flags anomalies, not as a decision-maker. Deploy them where a wrong call is cheap and visible.
  • For regulated environments: a model that can say "insufficient evidence" is the behaviour regulators will want to see documented. Ask vendors for their rate of appropriate abstention, not just accuracy.
  • For the broader AI-for-science push: benchmarks built from raw evidence rather than curated figures are the right direction. Expect rivals to publish comparable tests, and expect the gap between reading data and making sound decisions to be the thing that closes last.
